title: Auditing and Database Activity
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of auditing and database activity.
Apply audit event concepts in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.
Validate the result against the expected behavior and identify one portability, safety, or edge-case consideration.

content.intro: Learn auditing and database activity through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Auditing and Database Activity matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: The goal of auditing and database activity is to reduce what identities and queries are allowed to do. Apply defense in depth: parameterize values, grant least privilege, protect sensitive data, and verify denial cases as well as allowed cases.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Audit event concepts, Tracking sensitive operations, Database logs, Identifying access anomalies. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Audit event concepts
items.text: Audit event concepts should be enforced at the database/application boundary rather than by UI checks alone. Bind data values as parameters, grant only the access a role needs, and test that unauthorized operations fail.

items.title: Tracking sensitive operations
items.text: Tracking sensitive operations begins with a definition of the metric and its grain. Name the numerator, denominator, time zone, null policy, and tie-handling rule before translating the definition into SQL.

items.title: Database logs
items.text: Database logs helps you apply least privilege, safe parameterized access, sensitive-data protection, auditing, and database-level isolation controls. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Identifying access anomalies
items.text: Identifying access anomalies is a modeling choice. Identify the facts, decide which table owns each fact, then use keys and relationship tables to reduce duplication while preserving the business meaning.

items.title: Audit retention and privacy
items.text: Audit retention and privacy should be enforced at the database/application boundary rather than by UI checks alone. Bind data values as parameters, grant only the access a role needs, and test that unauthorized operations fail.

content_blocks.code: SELECT pid, usename, application_name, state, query_start FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname = current_database() ORDER BY query_start DESC NULLS LAST;
content_blocks.expected_output: The view helps review sessions in the current database; which session details are visible depends on role privileges. Avoid logging sensitive query text.

content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

task_acceptance_criteria: The query or design example matches the lesson's intended behavior.
The expected row grain and relevant NULL, duplicate, boundary, or permission behavior are explained.
The test is performed only in the local disposable lab, or clearly marked as a static inspection when a real runner is unavailable.
hints: Begin with the subtopic audit event concepts and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.

summary: Auditing and Database Activity is about making the database behavior and the expected result explicit.
Use the provided subtopics as a review checklist and validate a small test case.
Keep vendor-specific syntax, access assumptions, and production-safety boundaries visible.
